title: First law of thermodynamics and p–V work; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Charge and current
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: T07-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; T07-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T07-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game; T07-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL01-1#N.3, T02-1#N.3a, T02-uk1#N.10b, T07-1#N.3b, T07-uk1#N.3, EL01-1#N.6a, T02-1#N.10, T07-1#N.9, T07-uk1#N.5, EL01-1#N.11, T07-1#N.10, T07-uk1#N.8.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Heating
items.clue: Energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference.

items.label: Work
items.clue: Energy crossing a boundary because a force moves it, as with a piston.

items.label: Cycle
items.clue: Closed path on a p–V graph back to the starting state: ΔU = 0, so net Q = net W.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Symbol U: random kinetic plus potential contributions of the particles; a property of the state.

questions.stem: In an electron beam in a vacuum tube, 1.5 × 10¹⁵ electrons pass through a cross-section of the beam in 8.0 s at a steady rate. What is the magnitude of the current in the beam? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.

A student uses the electrical method to find the specific heat capacity of a brass block. Her value is 10% higher than the data-book value. Which change to her method would most reduce this difference?

options.text: Repeat the experiment three times and calculate a mean value
Use a thermometer with a finer scale, reading to 0.1 °C
Wrap the block in thick insulation and put a lid of insulation on top
Use a lower heater power so the block heats more slowly

questions.explanation: Less energy escapes to the surroundings, so more of VIt raises the block's temperature. The value of c falls towards the true one.

questions.stem: A gas in a cylinder is supplied with 500 J of heat. At the same time it expands, doing 200 J of work on the piston. Using ΔU = Q − W, where W is the work done by the gas, what is the change in internal energy ΔU of the gas?
questions.explanation: Q = +500 J (supplied), W = +200 J (done by the gas). ΔU = 500 − 200 = +300 J.

questions.stem: A sample of ideal monatomic gas in state A has pressure p₀ and volume V₀. It is heated at constant pressure until its volume is 2V₀ (state B), then heated at constant volume until its pressure is 3p₀ (state C). Using ΔU = Q − W, what is the total energy transferred to the gas by heating from A to C?

options.text: 7.5p₀V₀
6.5p₀V₀
8.5p₀V₀
10.5p₀V₀

questions.explanation: ΔU = 1.5 × (3p₀ × 2V₀ − p₀V₀) = 7.5p₀V₀. W = p₀ × (2V₀ − V₀) = p₀V₀ (none during B → C). Q = 7.5 + 1 = 8.5p₀V₀.

questions.stem: Predict first. A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly towards the positive terminal of the cell.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, from the positive terminal towards the negative one.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.explanation: In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons. Being negative, they are attracted towards the positive terminal, and on average they drift only slowly (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water and 0.20 kg of cooking oil, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 12 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: water 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, oil 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?

options.text: The oil ends at 50 °C and the water at about 34 °C.
The water ends at 50 °C and the oil at about 34 °C.
They end at the same temperature, as each gets 12 kJ.
The oil ends at 30 °C and the water at about 14 °C.

questions.stem: A sample of 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic ideal gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 80 °C. The thermal energy supplied is 2.49 × 10³ J. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
In one process, a gas has Q = −120 J and W = −200 J, using ΔU = Q − W with W the work done by the gas. Which description is correct?

options.text: The gas expands, takes in 120 J by heating, and its temperature falls.
The gas expands, gives out 120 J by heating, and its temperature rises.
The gas is compressed, gives out 120 J by heating, and its temperature rises.
The gas is compressed, gives out 120 J by heating, and its temperature falls.

questions.explanation: ΔU = −120 − (−200) = +80 J. More energy enters as work (200 J) than leaves by heating (120 J), so U and T rise.

questions.stem: Several wires meet at a junction in a circuit with steady currents. A student measures a current of 1.20 A in one wire leading into the junction, and currents of 0.70 A and 0.40 A in two wires leading out of it. The ammeters are ideal and read correctly. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The other wires at the junction carry a net current of 0.10 A away from it.
0.10 A of the current was used up as charge passed through the junction.
Charge is building up at the junction at a rate of 0.10 C each second.
An unmeasured wire must carry 2.30 A, the sum of the three measured currents.

questions.stem: An ideal gas is in a cylinder whose walls and piston are perfectly insulated. The gas expands, pushing the piston outwards. What happens to the temperature of the gas?

options.text: It stays the same, because no energy is transferred to or from the gas by heating.
It falls, because the gas does work on the piston and no energy enters by heating.
It rises, because the molecules move further apart and gain energy as they spread out.
It stays the same, because the fall in pressure exactly balances the rise in volume.

questions.stem: A heat pump warms a house. Its working gas goes round a cycle. In each cycle, 300 J of work is done on the gas while it is compressed, the gas does 100 J of work while it expands, and it takes in 600 J by heating from the cold air outside. How much energy does it give out by heating to the house in each cycle?
questions.explanation: ΔU = 0 over a cycle, so net Q = net W = 100 − 300 = −200 J. 600 − Q_out = −200, so Q_out = 800 J.
